title: Data for Afghanistan: Afghanistan Consumer Price Index (CPI) Report — October 2026
summary: Country: Afghanistan Source: Data for Afghanistan Please refer to the attached file. Summary: • Overall prices rose by +0.1% month-on-month and rose by +6.4% year-on-year in October 2026. Because the overall change was small, the split is shown in percentage points: food prices subtracted 0.2 pp and non-food prices added 0.3 pp. • Health saw the steepest year-on-year price increase (+16.4%). Spices had the largest decline (-12.1%). • Provincial variation was substantial. Kabul had the highest MoM inflation (+0.6%); Takhar the lowest (-1.6%). 9 of 20 provinces reported food inflation above the national average (-0.3%). 11 provinces reported a MoM decrease in food prices. • Annually, Sar-e-Pul faces the greatest cost-of-living pressure (+21.6% YoY). Parwan had the lowest annual rate (-3.9%), suggesting more stable prices over the past year. • Among non-food items, housing costs rose by +7.4% year-on-year. Health costs also rose sharply (+16.4% YoY), adding pressure on vulnerable households beyond food expenditure. Methodology: Please see page 8 of the report for methodology.

title: Data for Afghanistan: Latest Poverty Lines by Afghanistan Provinces, October 2026
summary: Country: Afghanistan Source: Data for Afghanistan Please refer to the attached file. Summary: Data for Afghanistan estimates that as of October 2026, the average monthly poverty line per person is 2,799 Afghanis . This comprises 1,670 Afghanis for food items and 1,129 Afghanis for non-food items. See the attached full report for provincial poverty lines. Methodology: Baseline poverty lines: Poverty lines are drawn from Afghanistan's Income, Expenditure and Labour Force Survey 2020 (IE&LFS; 2020), conducted by the National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA) and the World Bank. Poverty lines are estimated per person per month. The food poverty line is set at the cost of obtaining 2,100 kcal per person per day from a reference basket reflecting actual Afghan food consumption, priced at Central Urban (Kabul) prices in Q1 2019 (October–December 2019). Its value was AFN 1,330 per person per month. Non-food poverty lines are area-specific (14 areas covering 8 regions × urban/rural residence) and priced in Q1 2019 (October–December 2019) prices at the time of the survey (IE&LFS; 2020). South and West Central regions are classified as rural-only and have no urban poverty line. As NSIA publishes CPI data only for 20 provinces, we fill missing provinces' CPI with average provincial CPI by region. Please see the attached PDF report for more details on methodology.

title: UNHCR Albania Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Albania, Serbia, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR advocates for a strengthened national asylum system and contributes to further developing the capacity of government authorities to align asylum laws and practices with international and EU law. UNHCR works with municipalities to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers by improving access to livelihoods, social protection and local services. UNHCR’s work in Albania is supported by the EU-funded EU4Migration project and the PSMM3 Regional Programme. HIGHLIGHTS Socio-economic inclusion UNHCR continues to work with the municipalities of Korça and Gjirokastra to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers. This collaboration aims to address barriers to decent livelihoods and access to social protection rights and schemes. UNHCR also advocates for their inclusion in the local social care systems of both municipalities. Strengthening asylum decision-making In July 2026, UNHCR organized a workshop on drafting asylum decisions to strengthen authorities’ practical skills in fact-finding, credibility assessment and legal analysis. The workshop helped participants develop the skills needed to draft legally sound, well-reasoned and evidence-based decisions. It also promoted exchanges of experience and a shared understanding of asylum decision-making standards among participating institutions.

title: UNHCR Austria Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Austria, Afghanistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Türkiye, Ukraine, World Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Statistics for 2025 show a further decrease in asylum applications, with a total of around 16,700 asylum applications compared to 25,360 cases in 2024. In 2025, only 42 per cent were new applications, others included children born to refugees and repeat applications. The downward trend continued in 2026 with 6,500 applications by 31 August. Austria is among the top donors to UNHCR’s activities, while supporting the international responses to the needs of forcibly displaced people worldwide. HIGHLIGHTS 2 new AMIF projects granted The office successfully applied for 2 AMIF projects. Both the continuation of the quality assurance project “Bridge” as well as the new voluntary return project for protection holders from Syria (PARRS) were granted. 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention The Office highlighted the Convention’s enduring importance through a variety of projects. The Convention was discussed in the media, including in a radio series featuring the Head of Office. Stakeholders and multipliers, including teachers, students and NGOs, received briefings and materials on the Convention and refugee protection. The Office also participated in several events, including panel discussions, lectures and high-level meetings (see below), focusing on the Convention.

title: UNHCR Belarus Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Belarus, Afghanistan, Georgia, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Access to asylum: UNHCR works towards enhancing the asylum space and standardization of the state Refugee Status Determination Procedure (SRSDP) through capacity building and liaison with asylum authorities at country and regional levels. Self-reliance and inclusion: UNHCR promotes inclusive and sustainable integration aligned with the UN Country Framework 2026–2030, aiming to expand the access of forcibly displaced and stateless people to national social protection systems. Since 1 January 2026, UNHCR’s operations in Belarus and the Russian Federation have been consolidated under a Multi‑Country Office (MCO). HIGHLIGHTS UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework On 23 June, the MFA of Belarus and the UN Country Team gathered to present to both the diplomatic community and the business sector in Belarus, strategic directions of their commitments and priorities in accordance with the five-year UNSDCF. UNHCR presented its priorities, focusing on longterm solutions for integration, emphasizing the role of the private sector to support inclusion of refugees in economic activities and promote self-reliance. Protection Monitoring Missions In 2026, UNHCR conducted three field missions across Belarus to monitor the protection situation, engage with regional authorities and learn first-hand information from refugees and asylum-seekers. These missions included visits to state-run accommodation centres for asylum-seekers in Vitebsk and Gomel, as well as a joint mission with the State Border Committee to the Brest region at the Belarus–Poland border.

title: UNHCR Cyprus Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Cyprus, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, occupied Palestinian territory, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR provides legal and technical advice, monitors the asylum system and supports protection-sensitive implementation of the EU Pact. In the northern part of Cyprus, where no formal asylum system exists, UNHCR conducts RSD under its mandate and works with partners to help refugees and asylumseekers access their rights. Across the island, UNHCR maintains direct communication with refugee communities and supports access to legal counselling, psychosocial assistance, promoting inclusion and selfreliance. UNHCR works across Cyprus to ensure access to international protection, prevent refoulement and promote the rights of forcibly displaced and stateless people. HIGHLIGHTS Implementing major asylum reforms Cyprus is moving from policy design to implementation of the EU Pact. UNHCR provides legal advice during the adoption of the legislation and targeted training to asylum service officers, social workers, the judiciary, police and other key stakeholders to support fair, efficient and protection-sensitive asylum processes. Preserving legal and social counselling UNHCR is working with the Government to maintain essential counselling during institutional transition, helping avoid service gaps and ensure continued access to information, referrals and support. Supporting self-reliance At Kofinou Reception Centre, UNHCR supports the transition from reception to independent living through counselling, employment support and housing assistance, strengthening inclusion and easing pressure on the reception system. Building public support for refugee protection Through World Refugee Day initiatives and activities for the 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention, UNHCR supported community activities across Cyprus that promoted refugee participation, social cohesion and understanding of refugee protection.

title: WFP Indonesia Country Brief, September 2026
summary: Country: Indonesia Source: World Food Programme Please refer to the attached file. KEY HIGHLIGHTS • WFP advanced technical support to Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meals Programme, through cooperative guidance, fortified-rice policy and costing, beneficiary-targeting consultations, and South-South learning with Brazil and other partners. It secured government consensus on the fortified-rice costing study approach and institutional commitments for the next phase, while strengthening cooperative readiness, food safety and supply continuity. • WFP supported national and subnational institutionalization of Anticipatory Action through Aksi Merespon Peringatan Dini (AMPD; Early Warning Response Action), advancing the National AMPD Strategy and Guideline, Gunungkidul’s drought protocol and financing arrangements, and drought preparedness and village capacity in East Nusa Tenggara (NTT). • Gunungkidul operationalized its anticipatory action protocol and obtained legal clearance for a draft financing regulation, pending harmonization. In NTT, WFP and partners assessed six priority districts’ readiness, supported protocol guidance, began forecasting collaboration and launched village training for drought preparedness. SITUATION OVERVIEW • Indonesia is an upper-middle-income country with an annual gross national income of USD 5,120 per capita (World Bank, 2025). Despite substantial gains in poverty reduction and food security, alongside efforts to reduce inequality, malnutrition remains a concern. • Indonesia ranks 70th of 123 countries in the 2025 Global Hunger Index. Undernourishment fell from 7.2 percent in 2024 to 6.3 percent in 2025. The 2025 Food Security and Vulnerability Atlas identifies 62 of 514 districts/municipalities as vulnerable to food insecurity. • Gross domestic product grew 5.29 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while inflation had risen to 4.76 by February 2026. Food price pressures persist, particularly for volatile commodities. The ongoing El Niño is heightening drought risks and threatening agricultural production and food availability. • In 2025, Indonesia experienced about 4,727 environmental and extreme weather disasters—36percent higher than in 2024. Most were due to climate anomalies, impacting over 12 million people. • WFP Indonesia engages in policy dialogue and provides technical assistance to the Government of Indonesia in the context of food security, school meals, and climate and disaster risk management.

title: UNHCR Latvia Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Latvia, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR continues to collaborate with state authorities to improve access to asylum for those irregularly arriving in the southeastern regions bordering Belarus UNHCR supports the government of Latvia to strengthen protection measures for forcibly displaced people while aligning with the goals of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum HIGHLIGHTS Implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum UNHCR supports the Latvian government in its implementation of the EU Pact through advocacy and capacity building and by providing recommendations on draft legislation in the areas of vulnerability screening, detention, legal aid and counselling, as well as the national monitoring mechanism. title: UNHCR Romania Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Romania, Afghanistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR supports the government’s response to protect and include refugees in Romania through initiatives fostering inclusion and self-reliance, protection services, counselling and targeted assistance. Romania granted access to social benefits for refugees from Ukraine, through the Emergency Ordinance No. 96 on 28 June 2024, thereby addressing the needs of vulnerable refugees, to the same extent as Romanian citizens. UNHCR leads Inter-Agency coordination, supporting the national response, with 43 Refugee Response Plan partners ensuring alignment and synergy with the Government’s policy and localization. HIGHLIGHTS Life-saving assistance So far in 2026, UNHCR distributed 4,998 core relief items (CRIs), including blankets, bedding, clothing, and hygiene kits to 631 people in need. Protection information and counselling In 2026, UNHCR and partners have provided over 6,148 refugees with information and counselling in person or by phone. In addition, some 21,200 refugees are regularly reached through social media dedicated channels, including UNHCR’s Telegram channel, amplifying UNHCR’s messages to nearly 80,000 refugees. Delivering together UNHCR hosts 12 partners and national authorities at the RomExpo Community Centre in Bucharest, visited by over 100 refugees daily. The centre serves as a main “one-stop shop” for refugees. UNHCR is also hosting the social shop run by the Municipality of Bucharest.

title: Flash floods cut families off from healthcare in Mudug, Somalia
summary: Country: Somalia Source: Médecins Sans Frontières Flash flooding from heavy Deyr rains has affected more than 20,000 households in Galmudug, including in Galkayo, according to the state authorities. In Galkayo, floodwater has cut roads across the town, making it harder and more expensive for families to reach MSF-supported Mudug Regional Hospital and Galkayo TB Hospital. Cases of acute watery diarrhoea at MSF-supported facilities in Mudug more than doubled, from 356 in October 2025 to 748 in October 2026, and two cholera cases have been confirmed at Mudug Regional Hospital. Nearly two in three children admitted to the inpatient malnutrition ward in early November had acute watery diarrhoea. Our teams have expanded the ward from 28 to 70 beds, strengthened disease surveillance, trained staff on cholera, dengue and measles, and are reinforcing our capacity to treat cholera cases. ​ Flash floods are hitting towns across central Somalia, yet flood preparedness and limited available funding focus mainly on river flooding. Repairs In places such as Mudug, resources for responding to flash floods remain insufficient, leaving little for the drainage, safe water and sanitation that would protect families’ access to healthcare through the next rains. Humanitarian funding cuts are also leaving families across Somalia further from care. MSF calls on donors to make flexible funding available for the wider response to flash floods in areas such as Mudug, not only to riverine floods. MSF also calls on health authorities and humanitarian organisations to strengthen a coordinated response to urgent health, water and sanitation needs, and to invest in health facilities that can keep functioning through future floods. Families in Galkayo should not lose access to healthcare because the flood that reached them came from heavy rain rather than a river. For 15 days, Farhia Hassan Aden’s 18-month-old son had been vomiting and had diarrhoea. There is no clinic in her village in Mudug region, and since the October rains the motorised rickshaws that carry families to hospital have not been able to get through the water. The fare, US$4 to 5, was more than the family could pay. So Farhia walked through the floodwater with her son to Mudug Regional Hospital in Galkayo, which Doctors Without Borders/ Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) supports. He was admitted. “It forced us to walk in the water with our sick children,” she says. Farhia’s family is one of many caught by flash flooding since the Deyr rains began in October, in a year of El Niño conditions. In one week in October, more than 20,000 households were affected across Galmudug, including in Galkayo district, according to the authorities. Cut off and falling ill For five days, Bisharo Badal Yusuf could not get her 14-month-old son to hospital. He was vomiting and had diarrhoea, but floodwater had cut the roads. “We are cut off, which has forced families to keep sick children at home,” she says. “I eventually brought him to the hospital in critical condition.” Two days into his treatment, his fever had come down. Standing floodwater is also making people ill. Toilets have overflowed, floodwater has mixed with sewage, and the stagnant water that collects between houses fills with flies and mosquitoes. “The children are constantly scratching, and insects are swarming around them,” says Farhia. What our teams are seeing In October 2026, our teams recorded 748 cases of acute watery diarrhoea at MSF-supported facilities in Mudug, more than double the 356 in October 2025. Some patients have travelled more than 200 kilometres for care. In early November, admissions to the inpatient malnutrition ward at Mudug Regional Hospital were almost double last year’s, and nearly two in three children admitted had acute watery diarrhoea. We have expanded the ward from 28 to 70 beds. MSF works alongside the Ministry of Health at Mudug Regional Hospital and Galkayo Hospital, supporting emergency, maternity, neonatal and paediatric care, treatment for children with severe acute malnutrition, tuberculosis care and community health activities, all free of charge. Since the rains began, we have added staff, strengthened disease surveillance, trained teams on cholera, dengue and measles, and put supplies in place. Two cholera cases have now been confirmed at Mudug Regional Hospital. With the health authorities, our teams are strengthening cholera case management and sending mobile clinics to the communities hit hardest. Fewer places to turn For a family that, in Farhia’s words, “cannot even afford a single tablet of medicine”, each closure means a longer journey and a higher fare, and free care far away can be out of reach even before the roads flood. “Funding has been shrinking across the whole of Somalia, and access to healthcare with it,” says Dr Janvier Bahati, MSF project medical referent in Mudug. “In the long run, El Niño will make the current situation worse, reducing people’s capacity to cope, to the point where they are vulnerable to disease and malnutrition.” What families are asking for Asked what would help, the mothers we spoke to named simple things. Farhia wants the mosquitoes sprayed and the floodwater pumped out. Bisharo wants sanitation improved and “channels for the water”. “What the humanitarian actors need to focus on is to make sure that communities far away, and those affected by the flood, also have access to services,” says Bahati. “For me, that is the call: a drainage system across the city, chlorination of water and distribution of Aquatabs at community level.” Yet flood preparedness has focused largely on the river basins, leaving little for drainage, safe water and sanitation in places such as Mudug. MSF calls on donors to make flexible funding available for the wider response to flash floods in areas such as Mudug, not only to riverine floods. MSF also calls on health authorities and humanitarian organisations to strengthen a coordinated response to urgent health, water and sanitation needs, and to invest in health facilities that can keep functioning through future floods. title: WFP South Sudan Country Brief (November 2026)
summary: Country: South Sudan Source: World Food Programme Please refer to the attached file. Assistance and access: WFP reached about half a million people, distributed 2,343 metric tonnes of food and transferred USD 1.58 million in cash. Insecurity delayed deliveries in parts of Upper Nile and Jonglei, and reduced air transport capacity from November threatens deliveries to remote communities. Famine prevention: WFP had funding from November for only three of six priority counties: Ulang, Nasir and Nyirol. Uror, Fangak and Akobo still lacked funding for the response. WFP reported an overall funding shortfall of USD 388 million for October 2026–March 2027. Acute malnutrition: October surveys recorded rates of 28.3% in Fangak and 22.8% in Leer, both above the 15% emergency threshold. In Akobo, WFP worked with UNICEF and IRC to keep 14 supplementary feeding sites operating through December.

title: UNHCR Spain Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Spain, Colombia, Ukraine, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), World Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. From 1 January to 31 August, 20,417 people arrived in Spain by sea and land, 13% fewer than during the same period in 2025. Around 75% arrived through the Western Mediterranean route, while 25% arrived through the West Africa Atlantic route. During the first five months of 2026, around 50,300 people applied for asylum in Spain, 22% fewer than during the same period in 2025. The main nationalities were Venezuelan (58%), Malian (15%) and Colombian (7%). As of 31 May 2026, Spain had received 274,597 applications for temporary protection since March 2022, including 2,222 applications during January–May 2026. Of the applications submitted in 2026, 41% were from men, 41% from women, 10% from boys and 8% from girls. HIGHLIGHTS Queen Letizia of Spain receives UNHCR delegation and refugees Queen Letizia of Spain received a UNHCR delegation at the Zarzuela Palace, accompanied by refugees supported by UNHCR. The audience focused on the situation of refugees and asylum-seekers in Spain and UNHCR’s work to promote their rights and access to international protection. Read more here. Other stories: UNHCR served on the jury of a storytelling competition for refugee and migrant women organized by Nebrija Global Chair on Spanish as a language of migrants and refugees, helping promote women’s refugee voices through literature. The initiative culminated in a publication of selected stories featuring a foreword by UNHCR.

title: Sudan: Protection Cluster Alert : Escalating Conflict, Mass Displacement and Protection Risks in Blue Nile State - 27 November 2026
summary: Country: Sudan Sources: Child Protection Area of Responsibility, Gender Based Violence Area of Responsibility, Housing, Land, and Property Area of Responsibility, Mine Action Area of Responsibility, Protection Cluster Please refer to the attached file. The Sudan Protection Cluster is publishing a Protection Alert on the escalating conflict, mass displacement and deteriorating protection situation in Blue Nile State, dated 27 November 2026. The intensification of hostilities since early November has resulted in the displacement of approximately 47,460 individuals, with preliminary reports indicating an additional 22,467 individuals displaced, pending verification. These developments are exacerbating existing vulnerabilities and placing further pressure on already overstretched humanitarian services and reception capacities. The Protection Cluster is deeply concerned about the deteriorating protection environment, particularly threats to civilian life, safety and dignity, repeated displacement, barriers to seeking safety, heightened protection risks for women and children, explosive ordnance contamination, and increasingly constrained access to humanitarian assistance and essential services. The situation also underscores the importance of preserving the civilian and humanitarian character of refugee settlements. The alert presents an analysis of the evolving protection situation, recalls the obligations of all parties to the conflict under international humanitarian law, and outlines priority actions to prevent and mitigate protection risks and strengthen the collective humanitarian response. In light of these developments, the Protection Cluster calls for urgent and coordinated action to: Reinforce collective advocacy for the protection of civilians and safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. Ensure the continuity and scale-up of life-saving protection services. Strengthen protection risk mitigation across all sectors of the humanitarian response. Enhance contingency planning and operational preparedness for further displacement and potential deterioration of humanitarian access. Sustain support for local and community-based responders and safeguard their operational space.

title: UNHCR Sweden Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Sweden, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Asylum system: Sweden has made strong contributions to refugee protection through a well-established asylum system and policy support. The asylum system has been reformed in light of the implementation of the EU Pact as of the summer of 2026. Contributor of unearmarked funding: Sweden is UNHCR’s largest contributor of unearmarked funding. Sweden’s total contribution to UNHCR in 2025 amounted to USD 159.4 million. Stable and secure status: UNHCR advocates for Sweden to grant all beneficiaries of international protection a secure and stable status to facilitate integration. HIGHLIGHTS Fewer asylum applications and returns The Swedish Migration Agency reported that by August 2026, asylum applications in Sweden had fallen by over 40% compared to the previous year, while returns also decreased. These figures indicate a continued shift in the protection environment in Sweden, against the backdrop of significant policy and legislative changes affecting the asylum and reception system. UNHCR voluntary repatriation counselling Since August 2026, UNHCR has provided counselling services for refugees considering voluntary repatriation, funded by the Swedish Migration Agency. Through provision of independent counselling and reliable information on the repatriation process and conditions in countries of origin, UNHCR helps refugees understand their options and make informed decisions

title: UNHCR Switzerland Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Switzerland, Afghanistan, Eritrea, Ukraine, World Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. As of mid-2026, there are 211,381 refugees (96,201 with refugee status, 41,913 with complementary protection and 73,267 with temporary protection status S), 15,506 asylum seekers as well as 1,407 stateless persons in Switzerland. Switzerland estimates around 22,000 asylum applications for 2026 overall, down from 25,000 in 2025. UNHCR is engaged in the development of a new Asylum Strategy 2027 and works with authorities and NGOs to further strengthen the quality of the asylum system and the socio-economic inclusion of refugees. Switzerland remains a strong supporter of UNHCR, both as host of UNHCR’s headquarters and a top donor, providing flexible and predictable multi-year funding. HIGHLIGHTS A NEW CHAPTER FOR UNHCR SWITZERLAND AND LIECHTENSTEIN Since 1 July, the UNHCR Office for Switzerland and Liechtenstein has been operating with a significantly streamlined structure and now comprises only two staff. Despite limited resources, the Office continues to fulfil its core functions in dialogue, policy engagement and advocacy, monitoring developments in the asylum and refugee context, and fostering cooperation with government counterparts, civil society, academia, refugees, and other key stakeholders. PATH2WORK Path2Work became a UNHCR-Partner. Through the partnership between Path2Work and UNHCR, bridges are being built between refugee talent and employers, creating new career opportunities and laying the foundations for sustainable integration. Currently, 15,000 users are registered on the digital platform, with a further 17,000 people set to be invited to join from October. Access to the labour market fosters self-reliance, inclusion, and meaningful participation in society.

title: Safe, Dignified and Gender-Responsive Sanitation for Humanitarian Demining Operations in Ukraine
summary: Country: Ukraine Source: WeWorld Please refer to the attached file. Together with The HALO Trust , WeWorld conducted an assessment of sanitation facilities used by personnel involved in humanitarian mine action in Ukraine . The report examines how these facilities meet staff needs, highlighting the importance of privacy, hygiene, safety and gender-responsive infrastructure, including provisions for menstrual health and hygiene. As more women take on operational roles in mine action, ensuring that field facilities respond to the needs of all personnel is increasingly important. Through this assessment, WeWorld aims to support practical improvements to working conditions and contribute to wider efforts to integrate WASH, gender and dignity into humanitarian mine action.

title: The Systems Beneath Recovery: What WASH in Health Reveals About Recovery Readiness in Ukraine
summary: Country: Ukraine Source: WeWorld Please refer to the attached file. What does it take to rebuild a health system that can withstand future shocks, respond to changing needs and provide quality care for everyone? This report explores that question through a lens that is often overlooked in discussions on reconstruction: water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in healthcare settings. Drawing on nearly five years of WeWorld’s experience in Ukraine, this report argues that WASH in Health is far more than a technical or infrastructure issue. Reliable water supply, sanitation, hygiene, waste management and accessible environments are fundamental to quality care, infection prevention, preparedness and resilience. The findings show that rebuilding infrastructure alone is not enough. Sustainable recovery depends on strong management, adequate funding and regular maintenance, alongside practical tools such as WASH FIT to support planning and decision-making. Resilient healthcare also requires prepared staff, reliable backup systems and accessible, inclusive services, particularly as the needs of persons with disabilities and veterans continue to grow. Ultimately, this publication shows that how essential systems are managed and maintained today will shape the quality and resilience of healthcare in the years to come.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Country: Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Life-saving assistance & protection: UNHCR delivers critical humanitarian assistance and protection to evacuated and other newly displaced people, as well as to war-affected people in frontline areas facing hostilities, and those impacted by aerial attacks. Supporting IDPs with vulnerabilities in protracted displacement: UNHCR provides protection services and humanitarian assistance to IDPs through targeted programmes to promote access to rights, dignified accommodation, and durable solutions. Durable solutions and recovery: UNHCR contributes to recovery and durable solutions through community based, psychosocial, and legal protection programmes, repair of homes and support to access inclusive social protection services. HIGHLIGHTS Emergency shelter: Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, UNHCR has supported over 665,000 people across the country with emergency shelter kits and materials immediately after attacks. For more info, see the 2026 Q2 Shelter & Housing Factsheet here. Cash assistance is one of the most efficient and effective ways to support people adversely impacted by the war in Ukraine. Between January - August 2026, UNHCR disbursed multipurpose cash assistance to almost 128,478 people with specific needs. Since March 2022, UNHCR has provided cash assistance to more than 2.5 million people in Ukraine, totaling $748 million. For more info, see the 2026 Q2 Cash Assistance Factsheet here. Winter response: To prevent further displacement and help people remain safe and warm in their homes, UNHCR launched a comprehensive winter response plan for 2026-27 as a part of a broader UN inter-agency appeal.
